sb_prompt: SEE HOW THE OTHER CALLER FEELS ABOUT THE PROPOSAL THAT ALL YOUNG AMERICANS SHOULD SPEND A YEAR OR TWO DOING SOME KIND OF PUBLIC SERVICE
raw_output:
ParticipantA: Hello!
ParticipantB: Hello!
ParticipantA: Hi, I just got your number from the study group.
ParticipantB: Oh, hey. Yeah, me too.
ParticipantA: They said you're the bus driver guy from the survey?
ParticipantB: That's me. Yeah, I drive the 74 route in the south side.
ParticipantA: Oh, cool. I'm the manager at the grocery store on 4th.
ParticipantB: Oh, nice. So we're both kind of in service jobs, I guess.
ParticipantA: Yeah, pretty much. Anyway, they wanted us to chat about this whole "year or two of public service for young Americans" thing.
ParticipantB: Right. That's the proposal. Everyone has to do it before they turn twenty-five or something.
ParticipantA: Yeah. So, what do you think? You've been driving buses for how long?
ParticipantB: Three years now. Just turned three last month.
ParticipantA: Okay. So you've seen a lot of kids on that route?
ParticipantB: Yeah, every day. Some are really into it, some are just going to school because they have to.
ParticipantA: Yeah, that's what I was thinking. I've been at the store for ten years, so I've seen the kids come and go.
ParticipantB: True. I mean, some of them come back later too.
ParticipantA: Exactly. And you know, I've given this thing some thought for a while.
ParticipantB: Yeah, me too. It's been on my mind since they started talking about it.
ParticipantA: Yeah. I mean, on one hand, it sounds great. Kind of noble, right?
ParticipantB: Totally. It could teach them a lot about the world outside their own neighborhood.
ParticipantA: Yeah. But then I think... I just don't know.
ParticipantB: Yeah, me either. It feels like... well, it feels like we're just dumping a bunch of young people in a place they don't know.
ParticipantA: That's exactly it. I mean, they're just kids. They don't know what they're getting into.
ParticipantB: Right? Like, what if they hate it? What if they want to be an artist or something?
ParticipantA: Yeah, that's what I feel. It's not really their choice, is it? It's just... forced.
ParticipantB: Yeah, forced. It feels a little bit like the old kind of military draft, but for everyone.
ParticipantA: Oh, that's a good way to put it. Forced service.
ParticipantB: Yeah. And then, do you know, you're working in a grocery store. Do you see any of those kids hanging around the store?
ParticipantA: Not really. Most of them just pass through to get their lunch.
ParticipantB: Yeah, same here. Kids come on the bus, sit in the back, maybe talk to a friend. Then they leave.
ParticipantA: Right. They don't really need a year of it. They need to figure things out on their own, mostly.
ParticipantB: Yeah. I mean, I see some of them struggling in school. But I think they're figuring it out.
ParticipantA: Yeah. I think it's okay to struggle, to make mistakes.
ParticipantB: Yeah. I don't want to just lock them into a program that doesn't work for them.
ParticipantA: Right. It's not their life. It's the government's idea.
ParticipantB: Exactly. And what if they just want to work at the store for a few years, save up some money?
ParticipantA: Oh, that's a good point. I don't want to ruin their chance to make their own money.
ParticipantB: Yeah. They could go to a community college, work part-time, learn a trade.
ParticipantA: Yeah. It's about responsibility, I think. Not forcing it, but letting them choose.
ParticipantB: Right. If they want to help, great. But if they don't, let them go out and find their own way.
ParticipantA: Yeah. I think that's the real issue. It's not about the service, it's about the choice.
ParticipantB: Yeah. I think that's a good way to look at it.
ParticipantA: Yeah. So, do you think they should just scrap the whole idea?
ParticipantB: Yeah. Or maybe make it optional? Like a volunteer thing?
ParticipantA: Yeah. Let them opt in. If they really want to do it, fine. But don't make them do it.
ParticipantB: Yeah. I think that makes more sense.
ParticipantA: Yeah. It feels fairer, you know?
ParticipantB: Yeah. It feels more like... well, it feels like respect.
ParticipantA: Yeah. Respect for them. Respect for their future.
ParticipantB: Yeah. I think that's it. Thanks for talking it over.
ParticipantA: Yeah, you too. Good luck with the 74 route.
ParticipantB: Thanks. You take care at the store.
ParticipantA: Will do. Bye.
ParticipantB: Bye.
